zh: 固定一次累计位图，看任意一个 0：一轮从左到右的原地扫描里，只要它左边还有 1，离它最近的那个 1 会一路推过来和它交换，所以这个 0 每轮恰好左移一格。它需要的轮数就等于它左边 1 的个数。
整个位图排好序所需的交换轮数，是所有 0 左边 1 的个数的最大值，而这个最大值出现在最右边的那个 0 上；再加上最后一轮无交换的检查轮就是答案。若位图里已经没有 0，答案是 1。
维护一个标记数组和指针 last，表示当前最右边仍为 0 的位置（初始为 n，没有 0 时为 0）。第 k 次 ping 把对应位置标 1，然后只要 last 指向的位置已是 1 就把 last 左移。last 右侧有 n−last 个 1，所以答案是 k−(n−last)+1。指针总共最多移动 n 次，整体 O(n)；输入可达数百万个数，要流式读入、分块输出。
en: Fix one cumulative bitmap and look at any single 0. In one left-to-right in-place pass, as long as there is still a 1 to its left, the nearest such 1 gets pushed all the way along and swaps with it, so that 0 moves exactly one cell left per pass. The number of passes it needs equals the number of 1s to its left.

The number of swapping passes needed to sort the whole bitmap is the maximum, over all 0s, of the number of 1s to the left of that 0, and that maximum is reached at the rightmost 0. Add the final pass with no swaps and you have the answer. If the bitmap has no 0 left, the answer is 1.

Keep a marker array and a pointer last to the rightmost position that is still 0 (initially n, or 0 when no 0 remains). On the k-th ping, mark that position as 1, then move last to the left while it points at a 1. There are n−last ones to the right of last, so the answer is k−(n−last)+1. The pointer moves at most n times in total, so the whole thing is O(n); the input can hold millions of numbers, so read it as a stream and write the output in chunks.

explanationEn:
## Original rules and disambiguation from the sample

fastprep/Fortinet/fortinet-get-required-sweeps.md at the pinned commit e66f809f4c953bce129f68491726176615db6afc states that n binary signals start as all 0, and each position is pinged exactly once, turning it into 1. Each evaluation checks adjacent cells from left to right in order, swapping a 10 immediately when it meets one, and stops only after a full pass with no swap. The original sample ping=[1,2,4,3] returns [2,3,3,1] and is kept in full.

This site explicitly records two conventions disambiguated by the original sample: positions are 1-based and ping is a permutation of 1..n; and each time, the number of sorting passes is computed on a copy of the bitmap accumulated from the pings so far, so sorting never permanently changes the signal bitmap. If the previous sorted result were written back, the first evaluation would turn 1000 into 0001, and after the second ping 0101 would need only 2 passes, contradicting the original second value 3. The last bitmap, all 1s, is already sorted yet still returns 1, which makes it clear that the final checking pass with no swap is counted too. Left-to-right swapping happens in place and in order, so a single 1 can move past several 0s within one pass; the adjacent swaps are not all performed in parallel.

The old catalog editorial claimed that each 1 moves at most one cell right per pass, which does not match the original left-to-right in-place scan; its attached solution computed 3 instead of 2 for the first value of the original sample and also failed to count the stopping pass. This site rewrote the reference and the editorial instead of reusing that wrong implementation: one sweep over 1000 turns it into 0100, 0010 and 0001 in turn, so the same 1 really moves three cells right within one pass, and after a following pass with no swap the total is 2 passes.

The original gives no numeric upper bound on n. This site does not invent a limit such as 100000; instead it covers every valid permutation within the existing 32MiB standard-input budget: the first line is n, followed by n whitespace-separated integers in 1..n, each appearing exactly once. n=0 is accepted as an empty permutation and outputs an empty line; this is a mathematical extension disclosed by this site, not something the original states explicitly. The other public examples are derived by this site. The source image points to a file on the author's own machine; it was not used as accessible evidence, and no upstream code was executed.

## Approach

Maintain the bitmap of the cumulative pings and last, the rightmost position that is still 0 (or 0 if no 0 remains). With k positions pinged so far, the n−last positions to the right of last are all 1, and the remaining k−(n−last) ones lie before some 0. The answer is k−(n−last)+1. Each time, set the new position to 1 and keep moving last to the left until it points at a 0; over the whole run the pointer moves at most n times. Input and output are both streamed, and the answers are not all stored.

## Proof of correctness

Fix one cumulative bitmap and consider any 0. During one left-to-right in-place sweep, if there is still a 1 to its left, the 1 nearest to it is pushed right through the 0s along the way and finally swaps with this 0; after the swap the scan has already passed this 0, so the 0 moves left exactly once in this pass. If there is no 1 to its left, it does not move. So the number of swapping passes this 0 needs to clear every 1 on its left is exactly the number of 1s initially to its left.

The array is sorted if and only if no 0 has a 1 to its left. By the rule above, each 0 loses one blocker per pass, so the number of swapping passes equals the maximum, over the 0s, of the number of 1s to the left; this maximum is reached at the rightmost 0. Adding the final stopping pass with no swap gives the answer. If no 0 remains, the maximum counts as 0 and the answer is 1.

After the k-th ping there are k ones in total, and exactly n−last of them lie to the right of the rightmost zero, so k−(n−last) ones lie to its left. The bitmap records all and only the positions pinged so far, and moving the pointer left skips exactly the newly formed all-1 suffix, so the reference implementation computes exactly the answer proved above. The sorting effect of each round is defined only on a copy of the bitmap; the actual algorithm never destroys the original ping state.

## Complexity and transfer capacity

Time O(n), extra space O(n) bytes, and the output is printed item by item. Each position is written once and last decreases at most n times. Both n and the answers fit in 32-bit integers: n distinct positive integers forming a complete permutation within 32MiB of text give a maximum n of about 4333190, nowhere near the Java int limit. The original source has no upper bound; this is only a derivation from the existing transfer budget, and that number is not stated as an extra original constraint.

For step k<n the answer is at most k+1, and the last step is 1. Therefore the total decimal length of all answers is no larger than the total digit length of the input permutation 1..n, so the output budget never exceeds the digit body of an equivalent input. The reference runs with 3 seconds / 256MiB and a 64MiB output limit; the total size of the formal package is further bounded by import and Git file limits. Only one set of largest input and output cases is kept, to avoid stacking duplicates beyond 100MiB.

## Independent verification

The small oracle really copies the cumulative bitmap each time and loops over all adjacent in-place swaps until no swap happens, counting the passes directly; it does not use the rightmost-zero formula. 166 unique inputs (6 original/boundary examples and 160 random permutations from fixed seeds) were run through the native reference, and all 874 permutations for n=0..6 were also enumerated and run one by one. The medium-scale independent oracle tracks the remaining 0 positions with a max-heap and queries the number of 1s to their left with a Fenwick tree, which differs from the reference's monotone-pointer implementation.

The largest valid standard-encoded permutation is the increasing 1..n, whose answers in independent closed form are 2,3,...,n,1; for the reversed permutation all answers are 1. Other stress cases include random ones at the hundred-thousand scale, interleaved ones, and ones that ping the last position late, checking long suffix jumps and early-ping boundaries. All formal inputs are validated as permutations. The three negative controls respectively omit the stopping pass, use the zero's position instead of the number of 1s before it, and destroy the cumulative bitmap by keeping the sorted result; each must exit normally to count as killed.
